page: Microsoft Azure M8-2ms is a memory-intensive virtual machine from the MS server family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 2 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 1 physical core and 2 threads of an Intel Xeon 8280L processor operating at 2.7 GHz. The instance is equipped with 219.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-core ratio of 109.38 GB per core. It includes 262 GB of local storage and is premium storage capable, with zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses and no GPU hardware.

Benchmark data indicates a significant performance tradeoff. The instance registers in the bottom 10% for both single-core and multi-core CPU performance, with a stress-ng single-core score of 1019.69 and a multi-core score of 1351.6. Memory bandwidth is also limited, with read-only large block bandwidth at 9.62 GB/sec and write large block bandwidth at 8.08 GB/sec, placing it in the bottom 10% for memory throughput. Passmark memory benchmarks rate the memory subsystem as weak, scoring 1354.27.

Given the massive memory capacity paired with low compute performance, this server is designed for memory-bound workloads that do not require intensive CPU processing. It is suitable for large in-memory databases, caching layers, or data structures that fit entirely within RAM but experience low query concurrency. Qualitatively, the hardware profile offers high memory density per vCPU, making it cost-efficient for memory-heavy, compute-light deployments, though it exhibits poor performance in compute-heavy tasks like software compilation, image processing, and LLM inference.
description: Microsoft Azure M8-2ms is an x86_64 memory-optimized virtual machine featuring 2 dedicated vCPUs from a single physical Intel Xeon 8280L core running at 2.7 GHz. It is configured with an exceptionally high memory capacity of 219.0 GB, yielding 109.38 GB per core, and includes 262 GB of local storage with premium storage support. Benchmark results reveal a distinct tradeoff: while the instance provides massive RAM density, its compute and memory bandwidth performance fall into the bottom 10% across stress-ng, Geekbench, and Passmark tests. This makes the server highly specialized for memory-intensive workloads with low CPU demands, such as large-scale caching or in-memory data structures. Qualitatively, it offers high resource density for memory-bound applications but is inefficient for compute-heavy tasks like software compilation or real-time data processing.
